title: The Mark of the Wolf Man: from a Madrid furrier's workshop to the grave at Burgos
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Madrid, the furrier's workshop near the Plaza Mayor
stops.date_confidence: Birth date and city attested (es.wikipedia, 'Paul Naschy'; en.wikipedia; EcuRed). The Plaza Mayor workshop and the father's trade come from later profiles and Naschy's own retellings, not from any primary record located; the coordinate is the Plaza Mayor, not a documented address.
stops.campa: Enrique Molina cuts and stitches pelts in a workshop near the Plaza Mayor, for a Madrid that still has money to spend on furs. On the sixth of September a son is born to him and to Pilar Álvarez and is registered as Jacinto Molina Álvarez. The name will hold thirty-four years before a second one is manufactured for the export market. The child gets not quite two years of peace. In the third year the war shuts the trade down, and the workshop with it. The family goes out of the capital on the roads north.
suggested_refs: The Molina family furrier's workshop near the Plaza Mayor, Madrid, ruined by the Civil War

stops.name: A village in Cantabria, the father in the doorway
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The scene survives only in Naschy's own first-person retelling (El Duende interview, 2000); the village is never named in any source consulted, so the coordinate is a rough Cantabrian centroid and not a landmark. The date orders the segment and is not attested.
stops.campa: The family is displaced by the war and sheltering in a village in the north. A man comes through the door at night, armed, bearded, filthy from the road, running from an execution order. The child under the bed does not recognise his own father and hides from him as from a beast. Sixty years later, asked where his monsters came from, the man who is by then Paul Naschy gives this room as the answer and not a cinema. An alleged half-brother who denounced the father appears in the dossier and in no source that could be checked.
stops.quote: El primer monstruo de mi vida fue mi propio padre.
stops.quote_source: Paul Naschy, interview with Juan Luis Bahillo, El Duende (2000), revistaelduende.com/creador/paul-naschy/
suggested_refs: Naschy's account of the Civil War flight, as told to El Duende in 2000

stops.name: Burgos, the wartime refuge
stops.date_confidence: Attested that the family spent part of the Civil War in Burgos (es.wikipedia, 'Paul Naschy'). The precise years within 1936-1939 are not fixed by any source; the date is an ordering device.
stops.campa: The displaced family passes part of the war in Burgos, the Nationalist capital, a cold Castilian city of cathedral stone and requisitioned rooms. The boy is four or five. No source fixes which years of the war he spent here, and nothing in the record says what he did in them. The city takes its claim on him later and keeps it: a wife from Burgos, a fantastic film festival he helps found here in the nineties, a plot in the municipal cemetery on the western edge of town. He will not be buried in Madrid.
suggested_refs: Burgos, Nationalist capital 1936-1939, wartime refuge of the Molina family

stops.name: Madrid, the witch in the cinema
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. Naschy's own account, per the research dossier, names the witch of Walt Disney's Snow White as his first cinematic fright; the Spanish release date of the film was delayed by the Civil War and is not established, so the date is an ordering device only and the cinema is unidentified.
stops.campa: Before the wolf man there is a queen who drinks something in a cellar and comes out of it hunched and warted, carrying an apple. Walt Disney's Snow White reaches Spanish screens late, the war having stalled it, and the fright a small boy takes from it in a Madrid cinema turns into a vocation instead of a nightmare. Naschy names this witch, not a Universal monster, as the first image on a screen that ever put fear into him. He never says which cinema. He never says the year.
suggested_refs: Walt Disney's Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs, delayed Spanish release; Naschy's account of his first cinematic fright
sources: Research dossier, citing Naschy's autobiographical accounts (no fetched source located this pass)

stops.name: Madrid, Frankenstein Meets the Wolf Man
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. Naschy retold this founding memory repeatedly and varied his own age at the time between eight, ten, and eleven; the Spanish release or re-release date of the film is not fixed in any source consulted, and the cinema is unnamed. The 1943 date is the film's American year, used here to order the segment.
stops.campa: Lon Chaney Jr. changes shape on the screen and Bela Lugosi meets him as the creature Mary Shelley wrote in Geneva a hundred and twenty-five years earlier. The boy comes out of that cinema fixed for life. Two monsters on one programme, neither of them defeated cleanly, both of them more interesting than the men hunting them. He will tell the story hundreds of times over the next sixty years and never once keep his own age in it straight: eight, he says, and then ten, and then eleven.
suggested_refs: Universal's Frankenstein Meets the Wolf Man (1943), the founding image of the Daninsky cycle
sources: Research dossier synthesis of Naschy's repeated first-person accounts

stops.name: Gimnasio Guzmán el Bueno, Madrid: the first weights
stops.date_confidence: Attested that he trained at the Guzmán el Bueno gym (proyectonaschy.com, 'Jacinto Molina y su primera pasión: la halterofilia'); the starting year is not given and the date orders the segment.
stops.campa: The boy who wanted to look like a monster settles for looking like a man who could fight one. He begins lifting at the Guzmán el Bueno gym, in a Madrid where organised sport runs through parish clubs and company teams and the barbell is a poor man's apparatus. Nothing about this is a detour from the cinema. The physique he builds here is the reason producers will one day look around a room full of actors, fail to find a leading man, and point at the scriptwriter.
suggested_refs: Gimnasio Guzmán el Bueno, Madrid, first training base

stops.name: Gimnasio Juventud, Calle Fuencarral: the harder room
stops.date_confidence: Attested (proyectonaschy.com, 'Jacinto Molina y su primera pasión: la halterofilia'), which describes the move to a rougher facility without giving a year; the date orders the segment. The coordinate is Calle Fuencarral, not a verified street number.
stops.campa: He moves to the Gimnasio Juventud on Calle Fuencarral, a rougher room than the gyms of his adolescence, and trains there in earnest. Chalk, iron, a wooden platform, men who lift for the federation and not for the mirror. He is studying architecture, or beginning to, and writing westerns on the side; the gym is the only one of the three occupations he pursues without an audience. Within three years he will be national champion in his weight class.
suggested_refs: Gimnasio Juventud, Calle Fuencarral, Madrid

stops.name: Madrid, the Olympic weightlifting section of Real Madrid
stops.date_confidence: Attested (proyectonaschy.com, 'Jacinto Molina y su primera pasión: la halterofilia'), which credits him with records variously numbered at 28 and places the club's run of six consecutive national titles in this period; no primary club record was checked. The dossier's claim of a 295.5 kg total on 7 June 1959 could not be confirmed and is not asserted here.
stops.campa: He joins the Olympic weightlifting section of Real Madrid and stays with it for thirteen years. The team takes six consecutive national championships with him in it; his own record tally is given in the sport histories as twenty-eight, a figure no federation results book was produced to confirm. He retires from competition in 1971, at thirty-six. By then he has been a horror star in two languages for three years, and has kept the training up the whole time.
suggested_refs: The Olympic weightlifting section of Real Madrid, 1958-1971

stops.name: Valencia, Spanish champion at 67.5 kilos
stops.date_confidence: Attested (es.wikipedia, 'Paul Naschy', which states he was proclaimed Spanish champion multiple times beginning this year; proyectonaschy.com for the Valencia venue and the 67.5 kg class). The month and the exact venue within Valencia are not given; the coordinate is the city centre.
stops.campa: In Valencia, at sixty-seven and a half kilos, Jacinto Molina is proclaimed champion of Spain. Neither the month nor the hall is recorded; what survives is the class and the title. It is the first podium and there will be others, though no results book for any of them has been produced. He is twenty-three years old. He has published western paperbacks under a borrowed English name and has not yet stood in front of a camera. Of the several careers he is running at once, this is the only one in which a man's exact worth is settled in public by a scale and a bar.
suggested_refs: Spanish national weightlifting championship, Valencia, 1958

stops.name: Vienna, the international platform
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. Biographical profiles place him at the world and European championships in Vienna, reportedly sixth in Europe and ninth overall after moving up to middleweight; no official IWF results book was located to confirm any placing. The Wiener Stadthalle attribution is a researcher's inference from the championship's known host venue, not source-confirmed; the coordinate is the Stadthalle itself.
stops.campa: He lifts for Spain in Vienna, moved up a weight class, and the accounts that survive him say sixth among the Europeans and ninth overall. No results book has been produced. Around this platform stand the men whose names he will steal: the Polish champion Waldemar Baszanowski, whose first name he will hang on a werewolf, and a Hungarian whose surname he will file down into a trade name. Rome came and went without him, and Tokyo will too; the reasons given are a hand injury, crushed vertebrae, and federation politics, and no source reconciles them.
suggested_refs: The 1961 world and European weightlifting championships, Vienna

segments.name: Jack Mills, and the Back of the Set

stops.name: Madrid, Ediciones Rollán buys the western
stops.date_confidence: Attested that Rollán published him under the house-imposed pseudonym (proyectonaschy.com, 'Paul Naschy, Jacinto Molina y Jack Mills', quoting his 2008 memoir). Individual titles and their years rest on bibliographic synthesis in the research dossier, not on inspected copies; one surviving copy is credited 'Jack Mill'. The publisher's street address is not given and the coordinate is central Madrid.
stops.campa: He writes a western, walks it into the offices of Ediciones Rollán without an appointment, and they take it. Three more follow. The house insists on an English-sounding name, so the novels go out as by Jack Mills, and at least one surviving copy has the s worn off into Jack Mill. Spain in 1960 wants its cowboys imported, or wants them to look it. The best of the four never reaches a shop. The censor kills it for sex and violence, and Molina does not get the manuscript back.
stops.quote: Escribí una novela del oeste titulada 'Yo sé que ganarás' y me presenté sin más preámbulos en una conocida editorial de la época: Ediciones Rollán. Aceptaron el manuscrito y luego llegarían otros títulos.(...) Eso sí, todos ellos firmados con un seudónimo aconsejado por la editorial: Jack Mills. Por desgracia la mejor novela que escribí me la tiró la censura por exceso de violencia y sexo
stops.quote_source: Paul Naschy, Cuando las luces se apagan (Ed. AISGE / T&B, 2008), as reproduced on proyectonaschy.com/2011/11/30/paul-naschy-jacinto-molina-y-jack-mills/
suggested_refs: The Jack Mills westerns of Ediciones Rollán, Madrid, 1960-1961

stops.name: Madrid, an Egyptian slave in King of Kings
stops.date_confidence: King of Kings attested (en.wikipedia, 'Paul Naschy': an uncredited bit part; revistaelduende.com specifies Egyptian slave and centurion). El Cid is [R]: it appears in the dossier but not in the English Wikipedia article and not on the El Duende page, and no source naming it was located this pass. The coordinate is central Madrid, not a shooting location.
stops.campa: Hollywood is shooting its Bible in Spain because Spain is cheap, sunlit, and full of men who will stand in a costume all day. Nicholas Ray's King of Kings puts Jacinto Molina in the crowd as an Egyptian slave and then as a centurion, uncredited both times. He is there to be a body, and he uses the standing-around to watch where the camera goes and how a stunt gets broken into pieces. The dossier adds El Cid to his extra work; the sources checked for this pass do not.
suggested_refs: Nicholas Ray, King of Kings (1961), shot in Spain

stops.name: Las Rozas de Madrid, the Bronston lot
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. That he worked as an uncredited extra on Nicholas Ray productions is attested (revistaelduende.com); 55 Days at Peking specifically is not named in the English Wikipedia article on him, contrary to the dossier's citation, and no source naming it was located this pass. The Las Rozas studio site is documented production geography, not confirmed as the site of his own work.
stops.campa: Samuel Bronston has built a studio city outside Madrid, and on its back lot the Legation Quarter of Peking stands in painted plaster while Spanish extras play the Boxer rebellion. Molina is somewhere in it, uncredited, one more body hired for the shape of him. The last of the great foreign productions to use Spain as a cheap continent is being shot around him. When the money leaves, the crews and the workshops and the lighting men it trained stay in Spain. He hires them in 1968.
suggested_refs: The Samuel Bronston studio lot at Las Rozas de Madrid
sources: Research dossier (attribution of 55 Days at Peking not independently confirmed)

stops.name: Madrid, La marca del hombre lobo and a name for export
stops.date_confidence: Attested: es.wikipedia, 'Paul Naschy' confirms the 1968 premiere and the name-origin story (Pope Paul VI plus the weightlifter Imre Nagy). A competing account, in proyectonaschy.com's weightlifting article, names a Hungarian lifter literally surnamed Naschy who won the 60 kg class; the two versions are not reconciled by any source and are both recorded here.
stops.campa: He writes a werewolf picture, and when the producers cannot get an ageing Lon Chaney Jr. and cannot find a Spanish lead, they look at the scriptwriter's shoulders and say: you. Enrique López Eguiluz directs, in seventy millimetre and three dimensions, and Waldemar Daninsky is born, named for the Polish champion Waldemar Baszanowski off the Vienna platform. For the export credit Jacinto Molina takes Paul from a newspaper photograph of Pope Paul VI, and Naschy from a Hungarian lifter. Which Hungarian is not agreed: one account says Imre Nagy, filed down, and another says a man already surnamed Naschy.
stops.quote: Yo convertí al hombre-lobo en una criatura salvaje, tremendamente erótica, incluso ambigua en muchas ocasiones.
stops.quote_source: Paul Naschy, interview, Miradas de Cine (December 2009), miradasdecine.es/2009/12/entrevista-paul-naschy.html
suggested_refs: La marca del hombre lobo (1968), dir. Enrique López Eguiluz, shot in 70mm 3-D

stops.name: Paris, the film that may not exist
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, and disputed. The whole episode rests on Naschy's own repeated account; no print, contract, festival record, or contemporary trade notice of Las noches del hombre lobo has ever surfaced, and filmographers disagree on whether it was completed. The date orders the segment. Coordinate is the canonical Paris pin.
stops.campa: The second Daninsky film is shot in Paris, Naschy says, under a director named René Govar, who then dies, taking the negative with him. No print has ever been found. No production company, no contract, no trade paper notice, no still. Filmographers list it, bracket it, or leave it out entirely. It sits in the middle of the cycle like a missing tooth, and the only witness to it is the man who says he starred in it. He never changed the story and never produced a frame of it.
suggested_refs: Las noches del hombre lobo, claimed 1968-69, dir. René Govar: no surviving print or production record
sources: Research dossier synthesis of film-reference works; status unverified in all sources consulted

stops.name: Madrid, marriage to Elvira Primavera
stops.date_confidence: Month and year attested; the day is contradicted between sources and the contradiction is not resolved here. en.wikipedia, 'Paul Naschy' gives 24 October 1969; the research dossier, citing a scholarly history of Spanish fantastic cinema, gives 4 October 1969. The date field carries the Wikipedia day.
stops.campa: He marries Elvira Primavera, of Burgos. The marriage lasts the remaining forty years of his life and produces two sons, Sergio and Bruno, who will both end up inside the work: on his sets, in his credits, on the plane to the New York convention, and finally in a courtroom after his death. Two sources give the wedding day and they do not agree, one saying the fourth of October and one the twenty-fourth. The month and the year are certain, and nothing in the record settles the day.
suggested_refs: Elvira Primavera, of Burgos, married to Jacinto Molina from 1969 until his death
sources: Research dossier, citing a scholarly history of Spanish fantastic cinema (conflicting day)

stops.name: Madrid, La noche de Walpurgis breaks out
stops.date_confidence: Attested by film-historical synthesis for the production year; wide release is generally dated to the following year. The Argentine and international release chronology varies by territory and is not resolved here.
stops.campa: León Klimovsky directs Naschy's script and the thing goes off like a shot. La noche de Walpurgis sells everywhere: Germany, France, Japan, the United States, where it arrives with the werewolf and the vampire woman promised in the title. A Spanish horror cycle now exists as an export industry. It exists because one weightlifter wrote himself a monster and would not give the part away. The money is real, and he says so without any of the modesty the trade expects.
stops.quote: Para el público es algo maravilloso, y yo me he forrado.
stops.quote_source: Paul Naschy, interview, El Duende, revistaelduende.com/creador/paul-naschy/
suggested_refs: La noche de Walpurgis (1970), dir. León Klimovsky, released internationally as The Werewolf Versus the Vampire Woman
sources: Research dossier synthesis of film-historical production and release chronology

stops.name: Paris, the Georges Méliès award
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. es.wikipedia, 'Paul Naschy' lists 'Premio George Méliès, Festival de Cine Fantástico de París (1973)', and biographical profiles repeat it, but no primary palmarès listing was located online. The month is unknown; the coordinate is the canonical Paris pin, not a named venue.
stops.campa: Paris gives him a prize named after Georges Méliès, the conjuror who first cut a woman in half with a splice. It is the first foreign honour of the horror career and it comes from the country whose fantastic-film circuit takes the genre seriously as cinema rather than as a market segment. Spain will take another twenty-eight years to hand him anything comparable. No festival palmarès listing this award could be found for this pass; the prize survives in his biographies and in his own account of it.
suggested_refs: Festival de Cine Fantástico de París, Premio George Méliès, 1973

stops.name: Sitges, best actor
stops.date_confidence: Attested: en.wikipedia, 'Paul Naschy' states he won Best Actor for Curse of the Beast at the October 1975 Sitges International Film Festival; es.wikipedia names the award for La maldición de la bestia. The prize name is given variously as Clavel de Plata and as the Silver Nail, and the discrepancy is not resolved. A direct fetch of sitgesfilmfestival.com/es/actualitat/palmares/1975 returned HTTP 403.
stops.campa: At Sitges in October he takes the best actor award for La maldición de la bestia. It is a jury of the fantastic giving a fantastic performer the prize an ordinary jury would never consider him for, in the one Spanish town where the genre is programmed as cinema rather than treated as a joke. He collects it while the Madrid critics are still writing him off as a bodybuilder in a rubber snout. What he thinks of those critics he says out loud, at the time and for the next three decades.
stops.quote: la crítica española es muy zafia, son gente muy frustrada.
stops.quote_source: Paul Naschy, interview, El Duende, revistaelduende.com/creador/paul-naschy/
suggested_refs: Sitges International Film Festival, October 1975, best actor for La maldición de la bestia

segments.name: Behind the Camera: Inquisitors, Murderers, and Japanese Money

stops.name: Madrid, Inquisición: the directing debut
stops.date_confidence: Attested: en.wikipedia and es.wikipedia and EcuRed all associate 1976 with the directing debut; general release is usually given as the following year. The coordinate is central Madrid, a production base rather than a confirmed shooting location.
stops.campa: He directs for the first time and casts himself as Bernard de Fossey, an inquisitor burning witches through a plague year. Franco has been dead thirteen months. The censorship that spent a decade forcing his scripts out to Bavaria, to the Carpathians, to anywhere that was not Spain, is coming apart, and the first thing he does with the freedom is bring the horror home to Spanish soil and put the torch in a Spanish churchman's hand. The film goes out generally the following year.
stops.quote: La censura nos obligaba a que las cosas ocurrieran en otros países.
stops.quote_source: Paul Naschy, interview, Miradas de Cine (December 2009), miradasdecine.es/2009/12/entrevista-paul-naschy.html
suggested_refs: Inquisición (1976), Naschy's first film as director

stops.name: Peñaflor, Sevilla: the Frenchman's orchard
stops.date_confidence: Release year settled at 1978 by es.wikipedia, 'El huerto del francés'; the earlier 1977/1978 database dispute is dropped. The underlying Peñaflor murders are dated by that article to 1898-1904, straddling the century line, so the film's basis is not a nineteenth-century case. The film's shooting locations are not confirmed as Peñaflor itself; the coordinate is the town the film dramatises.
stops.campa: In a Peñaflor inn between 1898 and 1904, gamblers were robbed, killed, and buried in the garden. Naschy directs the case and plays it straight: no wolf, no crypt, no full moon, only greed and a spade. El huerto del francés is the film that proves the horror star can act when nothing is chasing him, and the Spanish Film Academy will later name the performance among his strongest. Four decades on, Cultural Diversity Films restores it from prints that had gone to soup.
suggested_refs: El huerto del francés (1978), dir. Paul Naschy, on the Peñaflor murders of 1898-1904
Cultural Diversity Films restoration, presented at Sitges circa 2020

stops.name: Museo del Prado, Madrid: the Japanese commission
stops.date_confidence: The Prado documentary, its Japanese financier, and the reported 42-million-peseta budget are attested by revistaelduende.com, which gives no year. The geography lens dated it 1980 and the chronology lens dated the same Aconito activity 1981; the year is unfixed and the date here is an ordering device. The budget figure is Naschy's own claim, not an audited one.
stops.campa: A Japanese patron, Masurao Takeda, puts money behind Naschy and the actress-producer Julia Saly, and the werewolf director finds himself filming Velázquez and Goya for Japanese television. He gives the Prado documentary a budget he later reports at forty-two million pesetas, an unaudited figure of his own; no source fixes the year the thing was shot. For a few years the horror man is a maker of national cultural documentaries, paid in yen, working inside the Prado.
suggested_refs: El museo del Prado, Japanese-financed documentary, Aconito Films

stops.name: Palacio de Oriente, Madrid: the crews inside the palace
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The dossier cites a 1981 El País report on Japanese television crews filming inside the Palacio de Oriente; elpais.com could not be fetched this pass and the report was not read directly. The underlying Japanese-financed documentary activity is otherwise well attested.
stops.campa: Japanese television crews are admitted to film inside the royal palace, part of the same slate of cultural commissions. The Spain being packaged for Tokyo is the official one: throne rooms, tapestries, armouries, the state's own face. Naschy is inside it with a crew and a schedule. The country that will not give him a Goya is perfectly willing to be photographed by him for a foreign broadcaster, and he takes the work. No Spanish broadcaster had asked him for anything of the kind.
suggested_refs: El País, 1981, on Japanese television filming inside the Palacio de Oriente (not fetched this pass)
sources: Research dossier, citing El País (elpais.com fetch blocked this pass)

stops.name: Cueva de Altamira, Cantabria: the oldest painted animals
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The Altamira commission appears in the dossier's list of Aconito-era Japanese documentary work; no independent primary confirmation was located this pass and the date is an ordering device.
stops.campa: The documentary slate takes him to Altamira, in the province where he hid under a bed from his own father forty-four years earlier. On the low ceiling of the cave are bison drawn by people who lived among animals that could kill them and drew them anyway, in ochre and charcoal, by lamplight. The man filming them has spent his working life putting a hairy beast on a wall for money. Nobody in the record remarks on this and there is no evidence he did either.
suggested_refs: The Altamira cave paintings, Santillana del Mar, Cantabria
sources: Research dossier, Aconito-era commission list (no independent confirmation located)

stops.name: Tokyo, the samurai helmet
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, and weak. The Kurosawa meeting and the gift of a samurai helmet are Naschy's own uncorroborated anecdote (repeated on revistaelduende.com); no independent documentation of the meeting or provenance for the helmet was located, and no source fixes where or when it happened. The Tokyo placement and the date both order the segment rather than record a documented visit.
stops.campa: During the Japanese years, Naschy says, he meets Akira Kurosawa, and Kurosawa gives him a samurai helmet. The story has no second witness, no photograph, no letter, and no dealer's provenance for the object. He tells it as the authorisation for what he does next, which is to send his werewolf to sixteenth-century Japan. Whether the helmet ever sat in a room with both men in it is a question the record does not answer either way. The helmet itself has never been photographed.
suggested_refs: Naschy's account of meeting Akira Kurosawa and receiving a samurai helmet, uncorroborated

stops.name: Madrid, the beast against the samurai
stops.date_confidence: The film's existence, date, and content are attested by film-historical synthesis; the Kurosawa anecdote that Naschy attaches to it is not, and is flagged separately at the Tokyo stop.
stops.campa: La bestia y la espada mágica sends Waldemar Daninsky to sixteenth-century Japan, where a swordsmith forges silver and a wolf fights men who understand what possession means without needing it explained. Naschy writes it, directs it, and puts himself in the fur again. The cycle that began with a Universal double bill in a wartime Madrid cinema has now absorbed the samurai film, on Japanese money, fifteen years after the first transformation. He is forty-eight years old.
suggested_refs: La bestia y la espada mágica (1983), dir. Paul Naschy
sources: Research dossier synthesis of film-historical sources

stops.name: Madrid, Aconito folds and the father dies
stops.date_confidence: The father's death is dated 20 June 1984 (heart attack while fishing, age 74) by en.wikipedia, 'Paul Naschy'; this pass could not verify it against a primary record. The collapse of Aconito, the financial ruin, and the depression are Naschy's own memoir testimony. No suicide attempt is documented in any source; retrospective claims of suicidal thought are his own.
stops.campa: The Japanese financing ends and Aconito Films goes with it. In June his father dies of a heart attack while fishing, at seventy-four: the man in the doorway, the first monster, gone. Naschy's memoirs give the years that follow as debt, silence, and a depression he describes without embellishment. He keeps working through it at the level the money allows, and shoots Operación Mantis, a parody of the Bond films Ian Fleming's novels had set loose on the world twenty years before.
suggested_refs: Operación Mantis (1984), dir. Paul Naschy
Naschy's memoirs on the collapse of Aconito Films
sources: Research dossier synthesis of Naschy's memoir testimony

segments.name: The Howl of the Devil and the Opened Chest

stops.name: Madrid, El aullido del diablo
stops.date_confidence: Attested by film-historical synthesis for production, cast, and reception; the reading of the film as self-portrait is critical consensus rather than a documented statement of intent.
stops.campa: He writes it, directs it, and plays a failed actor haunted by the monsters he used to be, opposite his own young son Sergio, with Caroline Munro and Howard Vernon in the house. The film gives him every mask he ever wore and then makes him a man in a ruined mansion talking to them. Distribution is close to nonexistent; almost nobody sees it in 1987. Mondo Macabro will restore it for Blu-ray in 2021, thirty-four years later and twelve after his death.
suggested_refs: El aullido del diablo (1987), dir. Paul Naschy
Mondo Macabro restored Blu-ray edition, 2021
sources: Research dossier synthesis of film-historical and critical sources

stops.name: Madrid, the heart stops after training
stops.date_confidence: Attested: en.wikipedia, 'Paul Naschy' dates the near-fatal myocardial infarction to 27 August 1991 and the bypass surgery to 5 September 1991; the three grafts are his own later description. The city is presumed Madrid and is not stated outright by the source. The Spielberg telephone calls are Naschy's own account and are separately flagged.
stops.campa: He trains with weights, as he has since he was fifteen, and his heart gives out. He survives the infarction and goes under the saw nine days later for bypass surgery, three grafts by his own count. He is fifty-six. From the recovery bed he tells a story nobody has confirmed: that Steven Spielberg telephoned repeatedly while he lay there, and that he assumed it was a prank until his son checked the line. Nobody has produced a second witness for that. What is on the record is that he starts writing Waldemar Daninsky again from the recovery bed.
suggested_refs: The bypass surgery of 5 September 1991
Naschy's account of Spielberg's telephone calls (El Duende, 2000), uncorroborated

stops.name: Madrid, forty-five films at the Filmoteca
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The Filmoteca Española retrospective and the reported figure of 45 films come from institutional and press reporting synthesised in the dossier; no programme or press notice was fetched this pass, and no venue is specified, so the coordinate is central Madrid.
stops.campa: Filmoteca Española runs a retrospective and screens a reported forty-five of his films. The state archive of a country that will not nominate him for anything sits him down in front of his own catalogue: the wolf, the vampire, the mummy, the inquisitor, the hunchback, the murderer of Peñaflor. No programme or press notice for the season was located, and the count of forty-five comes from later reporting. He is fifty-eight, eighteen months out of open-heart surgery, and still working.

stops.name: Burgos, a festival for the fantastic
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, and the sourcing is weak. Later legal and obituary reporting summarised in the dossier credits him as founder or co-founder of a fantastic-film festival in Burgos; revistaelduende.com, previously cited for this, contains no mention of it, and no source naming Burgos was verified this pass.
stops.campa: In his wife's city, the city that took the family in during the war, he helps start a festival for fantastic cinema. He is fifty-nine. Having spent twenty-five years being the entire Spanish horror industry by himself, he begins building the thing he never had: a room, a screen, a jury, a place where the genre is programmed rather than dumped. The founding is credited to him in obituaries and in court papers. No source that actually says Burgos was verified this pass.

stops.name: Madrid, Licántropo: the wolf returns
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. Production, reception, and the best-actor prize at the Madrid fantastic film festival the following year come from dossier synthesis of production accounts; no primary festival record was checked this pass.
stops.campa: Licántropo: el asesino de la luna llena is written during cardiac convalescence and shot years later, a serious return to Waldemar Daninsky by a man who has just been reminded what his own body can do to him. Distribution is thin and the box office is poor, and the production accounts for it are second-hand. The Madrid fantastic film festival gives him best actor the following year, though no primary festival record for it was checked. He is sixty-one. He invented the character at thirty-three.

stops.name: Madrid, Memorias de un hombre lobo
stops.date_confidence: Attested by publication bibliographic data (Alberto Santos/Imágica, 304 pages, ISBN 978-84-920576-6-5, prologue by Christopher Lee); an English translation later appeared as Memoirs of a Wolfman from Midnight Marquee Press. The coordinate is Madrid, the publisher's city, not a verified address.
stops.campa: Three hundred and four pages, and Christopher Lee writes the prologue: the Dracula of Hammer introducing the wolf man of Madrid, one professional monster to another. Memorias de un hombre lobo is Jacinto Molina's account of Paul Naschy, and it is where a great many of the unverifiable stories in his life enter the record in his own handwriting: the lost Paris negative, the Kurosawa helmet, the childhood cinema. An English edition follows from a small American press.

stops.name: Manhattan, the Weekend of Horrors
stops.date_confidence: Attested for January 1998: Fangoria's Weekend of Horrors convention, the family trip, and the reception (proyectonaschy.com, 'Naschy: la conexión USA'), with El País coverage cited by the dossier. The exact day is not given. The Fangoria Hall of Fame induction by readers' vote is placed 'two years after' by the same source, resolving to 1999 or 2000 and not to a stated year. Coordinate is the Eighth Avenue hotel district, not a confirmed address.
stops.campa: Fangoria flies him to New York with Elvira and both sons. The queue for his autograph does not end. When the American press asks what all the noise in the lobby is about, the people in the line answer for him, and the answer gets into the Spanish papers. Almost nobody in that line has seen most of these films in Spanish; they know them under English titles his distributors invented. A readers' vote puts him in the magazine's hall of fame a year or two later.
stops.quote_source: Reported by Naschy in his El Duende interview as what onlookers told the press at a New York homage in his honour, revistaelduende.com/creador/paul-naschy/

stops.name: Washington, the Carl Laemmle award
stops.date_confidence: Attested that he received a Carl Laemmle lifetime achievement award in Washington alongside honorees including Roger Corman and Janet Leigh, coinciding with the English-language release of his memoir (proyectonaschy.com, 'Naschy: la conexión USA'); the source gives neither an exact year nor a venue within the city, so the date is an ordering device and the coordinate is the city centre.
stops.campa: In Washington he is given a lifetime achievement award named for Carl Laemmle, the man who founded Universal and green-lit the monsters that made him. Roger Corman and Janet Leigh are honoured on the same programme. He is standing in the country whose 1943 double bill set the whole thing off, holding a prize with the studio founder's name on it, being thanked in person by the industry that built the monsters he rebuilt. The source that carries all this gives neither the year nor the venue.
stops.quote: Mi etiqueta terrorífica me ha cortado caminos. [...] pero a mí, en mi tierra, se me ha limitado.
stops.quote_source: Paul Naschy, quoted in proyectonaschy.com/2010/06/01/naschy-la-conexion-usa/ (elision marked; the omitted clause compares him to Karloff, Lugosi, and Cushing, who could survive typecasting because their industry could carry it)

stops.name: Madrid, the Gold Medal of Merit in the Fine Arts
stops.date_confidence: Attested against the primary gazette: Real Decreto 159/2001, de 16 de febrero, published in BOE núm. 42 of 17 February 2001, names 'Don Jacinto Molina Álvarez (Paul Naschy), Actor'. The decree grants sixteen medals, thirteen to individuals and three to collectives or institutions. No ceremony is evidenced by the decree, which is a gazette act; the coordinate is central Madrid and stages nothing.
stops.campa: Real Decreto 159/2001 goes into the state gazette on the seventeenth of February and there, between a conductor, a couturier, a bullfighter, and a music festival, stands Don Jacinto Molina Álvarez (Paul Naschy), Actor. Sixteen medals in all, thirteen to people and three to institutions. It is the highest thing the Spanish state ever gives him. The decree evidences no ceremony; it is a gazette act, and the statuette he wanted from his own film academy never comes.
stops.quote: Soy consciente de que en España no me van a dar el Goya de Honor, pero tengo la Medalla de Honor de las Bellas Artes.
stops.quote_source: Paul Naschy, interview, Miradas de Cine (December 2009), miradasdecine.es/2009/12/entrevista-paul-naschy.html

stops.name: Hollywood Roosevelt Hotel, Los Angeles: two months of night shooting
stops.date_confidence: Attested: the roughly two-month stay based at the Hollywood Roosevelt and the two films, Don F. Glut's Countess Dracula's Orgy of Blood and Fred Olen Ray's Tomb of the Werewolf, are confirmed by proyectonaschy.com, 'Naschy: la conexión USA'. The month is not given and the date is an ordering device. Coordinate is 7000 Hollywood Boulevard.
stops.campa: He takes a room at the Hollywood Roosevelt with Elvira and Sergio, across the boulevard from the forecourt where the handprints are set in concrete, and works for two months on two direct-to-video pictures. Waldemar Daninsky transforms for the last time, at sixty-eight, on an American budget that would not have covered the catering on King of Kings. Neither picture gets a proper release in Spain. He is happier on these two cheap shoots than the pictures deserve, and says so to anyone who asks. The room is on Hollywood Boulevard and the work runs at night.
stops.quote: En Estados Unidos me siento muy a gusto, ya que he recibido una extraordinario trato humano.
suggested_refs: Countess Dracula's Orgy of Blood (dir. Don F. Glut) and Tomb of the Werewolf (dir. Fred Olen Ray), shot 2003

stops.name: Los Feliz, Los Angeles: signing Ackerman's Dracula
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The visit, the signing, and the ring are reported by proyectonaschy.com, 'Naschy: la conexión USA'; no independent confirmation and no exact date. The coordinate is Los Feliz, not a verified street address for Ackerman's house.
stops.campa: Forrest J Ackerman keeps the memorabilia of the entire genre in a house in Los Feliz, and among it a first edition of Dracula signed by Bela Lugosi, Christopher Lee, and Vincent Price. He hands it to Naschy and Naschy adds his name to theirs, wearing Ackerman's original Universal Dracula ring on his finger while he does it. Five names on the flyleaf now, four of them from the pictures a boy watched in a hungry Madrid in the years after the war. Ackerman, then eighty-six, has been collecting since before that boy was born.
suggested_refs: Forrest J Ackerman's collection, Los Feliz, Los Angeles

stops.name: Mission San Juan Capistrano, California: shooting at the mission
stops.date_confidence: Attested that scenes for Countess Dracula's Orgy of Blood were filmed near the mission (proyectonaschy.com, 'Naschy: la conexión USA'); the source says near, not at. No exact date. The coordinate is the mission itself, accurate to about a hundred metres; note that the mission is in Orange County, roughly 130 km north of the Mexican border, not near it as the dossier stated.
stops.campa: The unit works at the old Spanish mission at San Juan Capistrano, founded by Franciscans in 1776 and still standing in adobe and broken arch. A Madrid actor plays an undead count in a Californian church built by his own countrymen two hundred and twenty-seven years earlier, for an American producer, on a schedule measured in days. Whether anyone on that set noticed is not recorded anywhere. The source says the unit worked near the mission, not in it.

stops.name: Universal City, meeting Elena Verdugo
stops.date_confidence: Attested (proyectonaschy.com, 'Naschy: la conexión USA') for the Fangoria convention at Universal Studios and the meeting with Elena Verdugo, who appeared in House of Frankenstein (1944); the month is not given and the date orders the segment.
stops.campa: At a convention on the Universal lot he meets Elena Verdugo, who played the gypsy girl in House of Frankenstein in 1944, a year after the double bill that made him. The studio around them sells its monsters as a theme park ride now, and the two people standing in it who actually belong to that cinema are a retired American actress and a Spaniard who rebuilt the whole thing from scratch in another country because nobody would sell him the rights. She is eighty-two. He is seventy-two.

stops.name: Madrid, Cuando las luces se apagan
stops.date_confidence: Attested by publication bibliographic data: a revised, shorter memoir in the Memoria de la Escena Española series (Fundación AISGE / T&B Editores, 2008), with a closing text by Quentin Tarantino. The novel Alaric de Marnac, illustrated by Javier Trujillo and named by es.wikipedia as his sole novel, follows in 2009 and is folded into this stop.
stops.campa: He writes the memoirs down again, shorter and harder, for an actors' foundation series, and Quentin Tarantino closes the book. The following year he publishes his only novel, taking Alaric de Marnac, the sorcerer knight from El espanto surge de la tumba, off the screen and onto the page, with illustrations by Javier Trujillo. It is his only novel, and the first prose fiction he has published since the westerns a publisher made him sign Jack Mills. Both books go out while he is still working. The novel appears in the year he dies.
stops.quote: ¿Qué pretendía yo? Hacer cine fantástico, pues lo he hecho. ¿Interpretar al hombre-lobo? Lo he hecho.
stops.quote_source: Paul Naschy, interview, Miradas de Cine (December 2009), miradasdecine.es/2009/12/entrevista-paul-naschy.html

stops.name: Sitges, the last festival
stops.date_confidence: Attested in substance: obituary reporting (eldiario.es) situates his final public activity in this period and the Academia de Cine's later framing corroborates Sitges as central to his late recognition. The exact days of attendance are not fixed. The offered cameo in Joe Johnston's The Wolfman, prevented by scheduling, is a dossier claim from interview accounts and is [R].
stops.campa: Weeks from death he goes to Sitges, presents projects, and takes meetings. He is shooting for José Luis Alemán, La herencia Valdemar and its sequel, work he will not live to see released. Hollywood had asked him to bite Benicio del Toro in a remake of The Wolfman and the schedules would not meet, so the oldest working werewolf in the world does not appear in the last big-studio werewolf picture of his lifetime. He is asked at this time whether the genre has a future.
stops.quote: Tengo la seguridad de que el fantástico es eterno mientras exista la delgada línea roja que separa la vida de la muerte.
stops.quote_source: Paul Naschy, interview, Miradas de Cine (December 2009), miradasdecine.es/2009/12/entrevista-paul-naschy.html

La herencia Valdemar (dir. José Luis Alemán)

stops.name: Madrid, the death of Jacinto Molina
stops.date_confidence: Date and place attested: en.wikipedia, EcuRed, and eldiario.es agree on 30 November 2009 in Madrid, age 75. Some notices and the Real Academia de la Historia give 1 December because the death became public the following morning. The cause is contradicted and not resolved here: en.wikipedia says pancreatic cancer diagnosed in 2008; es.wikipedia says only cancer; the dossier's cited 2013 civil judgment says metastatic ductal adenocarcinoma of the prostate found during an unrelated operation.
stops.campa: He dies in Madrid at seventy-five, and his son Sergio confirms it to the press the next morning, which is why some notices carry the first of December. The papers say cancer. Which cancer they do not agree on: the general reference works say pancreatic, and a civil judgment four years later says a metastatic ductal adenocarcinoma of the prostate, found during an operation for something else, after years of rising readings nobody acted on. His widow and son go to court over the delay and win part of their case.
suggested_refs: The 2013 judgment of Madrid Court of First Instance No. 6, awarding 43,682 euros for loss of therapeutic opportunity
sources: Research dossier, citing larazon.es and elperiodico.cat on the 2013 judgment (not fetched this pass)

stops.name: Cementerio Municipal de San José, Burgos: the grave
stops.date_confidence: The cemetery is named directly in the es.wikipedia infobox and the burial date of 2 December 2009 comes from the same article; the coordinate is the cemetery at La Obispa, Burgos, per OpenStreetMap, and no plot is identified. Two earlier research passes gave two different and both incorrect coordinates for this cemetery; the correction is recorded in the report.
stops.campa: He is buried in the municipal cemetery of San José, on the western edge of Burgos: his wife's city, the city that sheltered the family in the war, the city where he helped start a festival. Not Madrid, where he is born and where he works and dies. Afterwards a wax Waldemar Daninsky goes up in a Madrid museum, American labels restore the films the Spanish distributors let rot, and a documentary about him premieres at Sitges in 2024, fifteen years after this burial and fifty-six after the first transformation.
